clue.text: Sign: ladies — no entry

indicators.note: the entry to a word is its opening letter, so having none means that first letter is dropped

parts.note: ladies are women, as on a toilet door

explanation.surface: A notice on the door of the women's toilets forbids anyone to go in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no entry' removes the opening W of WOMEN; the surface reads it as the wording of a door notice.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: a portent is a sign of what is to come.

clue.text: Essential to replace back of breeching in pack horse

indicators.note: the first piece is put in the place of a letter of the word for pack

parts.note: a pack is a gang, a group acting together

indicators.note: the back of a word is its final letter

parts.note: an essential is a must, something you have to have

explanation.surface: A harness strap on a load-carrying animal needs a vital spare part.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to replace' and 'back of' work together: the letter that ends breeching is the one swapped out. 'pack horse' looks like one phrase but splits between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: it is a wild breed of the American plains.

clue.text: There's nothing in Puccini? Listen!

indicators.note: the answer lies inside the run of letters of the next two words

explanation.surface: An opera sceptic claims the composer's work is empty, then tells you to hear for yourself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' marks a run of letters spanning the end of Puccini and the start of Listen.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym used for zero, especially in football scores.

clue.text: He's tight with a packet

indicators.note: tight is slang for drunk, so the letters stagger into a new order

parts.note: the letters H, E and S, taken as written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A man with plenty of money who hates spending any of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tight' (drunk) rearranges HES, A and PACKET, and the whole clue also describes the answer: a packet is British slang for a lot of money.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue is a description: a miser is mean even when holding plenty of money.

clue.text: Garden perhaps showing pear tree finally cropped

indicators.note: cropping cuts a piece off, so the letter is removed from the fruit's name

parts.note: Comice is a well-known variety of pear

indicators.note: finally picks the last letter of the word before it

explanation.surface: A plot of land displays a fruit tree that has at last been pruned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cropped' takes E, which 'finally' picks from tree, off COMICE. Garden is Graeme Garden, a British comedian from The Goodies, not a plot of land.
explanation.definitionFit: An example by name: Graeme Garden is a British comedian and funny man.

clue.text: Place for a plug close but nameless

indicators.note: nameless says the abbreviation for name, N, is taken away

parts.note: close means near, not far away

explanation.surface: A socket is not far off, but nobody has labelled it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but nameless' removes N (name) from NEAR. The plug is an earplug, not an electrical one.
explanation.definitionFit: A playful description: earplugs go in this organ of hearing.

clue.text: No good leaving stylist's division during employment for painter?

indicators.note: during means within, so one piece sits inside the word for employment

parts.note: a post is a job or position of employment

indicators.note: leaving says the two letters depart from the longer word

parts.note: a hair stylist divides the hair with a parting

explanation.surface: A hopeless worker quits a hairdressing department mid-contract to take up painting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving' shortens the hairdresser's word by two letters before 'during' places it within the job. The division is the line combed into hair, not a salon department.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: Warhol and Lichtenstein were painters of this movement, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Smacks taking on sailing vessels

indicators.note: taking means taking in, so the word for smacks swallows the next piece

parts.note: smacks are blows or knocks
on means about, as in a book on gardening

explanation.surface: Fishing boats pick a fight with other craft under sail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taking' is the container signal. Smacks look like fishing boats, a second set of craft, but here they are blows.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: they are small simply rigged sloops.

clue.text: High priest takes in a tramp

indicators.note: takes in means the rearranged word swallows the letter after it
high means intoxicated, so the letters of the next word are disordered

explanation.surface: A senior cleric gives shelter to a vagrant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High' rearranges PRIEST into TRIPSE and 'takes in' puts A inside it. The tramp is a verb, to trudge, not a vagrant.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym as a verb: both mean to trudge wearily.

clue.text: In which, heartlessly, you slam crackpot?

definitions.text: In which, heartlessly, you slam crackpot?

indicators.note: crackpot means crazy, so the letters before it are thrown into disorder
heartlessly removes the heart of the word, leaving its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A place where a mad person gets callously locked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heartlessly' leaves YU from you and 'crackpot' rearranges YU with SLAM; the whole clue is also the definition, in the old unkind sense of a mental hospital.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes it: historically an institution where the mentally ill were confined.

clue.text: Rocket on for very short meal? Count me out!

parts.note: on means concerning, which is re
pro means for, in favour of
V is the short form of very

indicators.note: out says the two letters of me are taken away from the word meal

parts.note: taken as written before the cut
taken as written, the letters removed

explanation.surface: Someone declines salad leaves offered as a tiny lunch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Count me out' removes ME from MEAL. A rocket is British slang for a severe telling-off, not a salad leaf or a missile.
explanation.definitionFit: A British slang synonym: to give someone a rocket is to reprimand them.

clue.text: Exceptional head of police getting about a joint

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

parts.note: articular means relating to a joint of the body

explanation.surface: An outstanding chief constable goes to investigate a seedy bar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head of' takes the first letter of police. 'about a joint' is one adjective, the anatomical word for relating to joints.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: special or exceptional, as in taking exceptional care.

clue.text: In sum, Russian money and power gets a place in the middle east?

definitions.text: a place in the middle east?

indicators.note: in says the following pieces sit inside the word for sum

parts.note: to sum is to tot, to add up
roubles are the currency of Russia
P is the physics abbreviation for power

explanation.surface: Moscow's cash and influence buy a foothold in the region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' opens the clue as the container signal. The question mark admits the Middle East is only one example of such a place.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: the region is often a scene of conflict and unrest.

clue.text: Set about reconstructing Italy? No

indicators.note: reconstructing means rebuilding, so the letters of the two words after it are rearranged

explanation.surface: Asked whether to begin rebuilding a whole country, someone refuses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reconstructing' rearranges ITALY and NO. 'Set about' means attack here, not begin.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: both phrases mean to attack someone vigorously.

clue.text: International for a short time retained cap

indicators.note: for means in place of, so the first piece takes the place of the second

parts.note: retained means kept
T is the short form of time

explanation.surface: A player briefly in the national side got to keep the cap awarded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' swaps I in place of the T of KEPT. A cap in the surface is an international appearance; the answer is real headgear.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: it is the flat-topped French military hat with a peak.

clue.text: One bargain single so long reported

parts.note: a single thing is one, or a

indicators.note: reported means spoken, so the farewell is heard rather than read

parts.note: so long is a way of saying goodbye

explanation.surface: News comes in of one cheap unmarried person taking ages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reported' turns GOODBYE into its soundalike GOOD BUY.
explanation.definitionFit: A paraphrase: a purchase that is cheap for what you get.

clue.text: One right to get involved in drunken spree? Wrong!

definitions.text: One right to get involved in drunken spree? Wrong!

indicators.note: getting involved in something means going inside it

parts.note: a bender is a bout of heavy drinking
one is a

explanation.surface: Is this the proper person to join a boozy night out? Certainly not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get involved in' is the insertion signal. The whole clue defines by denial: the person serving the drinks should stay sober.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes someone who pours the drinks and ought not to join the binge.

clue.text: At home Miliband embraces brother? It's natural

parts.note: in means at home
Ed Miliband is a British Labour politician, whose brother David was his rival for the party leadership

explanation.surface: A politician hugs a sibling in the family house, as you would expect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'embraces' is the container signal. Miliband famously beat his own sibling David to lead Britain's Labour Party, which gives the surface its bite.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: innate, present from birth.

clue.text: Cycle approaching traffic light in curve of the road

indicators.note: approaching puts the first piece just before the second

parts.note: c is the abbreviation for cycle, as in c/s, cycles per second
amber is the middle colour of a British traffic light

explanation.surface: A bike nears the signals on a bend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'approaching' sets C in front of AMBER.
explanation.definitionFit: A description: the slight arch built into a road surface so water drains off.

clue.text: Gunners coming from behind new area line

parts.note: behind is the bottom, in British slang the arse

explanation.surface: Artillerymen advance from the rear to a fresh front.
explanation.walkthrough: The Gunners is the nickname of a North London football club, which began at a munitions works.
explanation.definitionFit: A nickname: the London football club is known as the Gunners.

clue.text: What's nearly coming from me, perhaps touring desert?

indicators.note: touring means going round, so the first word travels round the second

parts.note: me is one note of the sol-fa scale
to desert is to quit, to abandon

explanation.surface: The speaker hints at what they almost say while travelling round the Sahara.
explanation.walkthrough: 'touring' is the container signal. 'me' is the third degree of the sol-fa scale, not the speaker, and desert is a verb meaning abandon.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: almost but falling just short.

clue.text: Scores made by Wigan forward in tests

parts.note: Wigan is a famous English rugby league club, and scores in rugby are tries
forward means on, as in from that day on

explanation.surface: A rugby player touches down repeatedly in international matches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wigan forward' reads as a rugby player but splits: Wigan, an English rugby league club, goes with the scores, and forward is a separate piece. Tests are trials, not internationals.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym as a verb: she tests a coat for size.

clue.text: The key is in passage American overlooked

indicators.note: overlooked means left out, so the letter is omitted from the word for passage

parts.note: an aisle is a passage between rows of seats

explanation.surface: What unlocks a text lies in a paragraph a US reader missed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'overlooked' drops A from AISLE. A key is a low island, as in the Florida Keys.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym in the geographical sense: a small low island.

clue.text: Virtually nothing stopping new ideas? No need for comment

indicators.note: to stop is to plug, so this piece goes inside the other
new means freshly made, so the letters of the next word are rearranged
virtually means almost all, so the word for nothing loses its last letter

parts.note: nought means nothing, zero

explanation.surface: Fresh thinking meets almost no obstacle, and nobody has to remark on it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Virtually' drops a final letter, 'new' makes ESAID, and 'stopping' is the insertion signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom meaning the point is made and further words are unnecessary.

clue.text: Pot shown by German novelist …

definitions.meaning: pot is slang for cannabis, which has this other slang name too
Günter, the Nobel-winning author of The Tin Drum

explanation.definitionFit: A slang name for marijuana and the surname of the writer of The Tin Drum.

clue.text: Pens said to work to a high degree

indicators.note: working something means manipulating it, so the letters of the two words before are rearranged

explanation.surface: Writing instruments are claimed to perform extremely well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to work' rearranges PENS and SAID.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom from bridge, where that suit ranks highest: in abundance, extremely.

clue.text: … So push bicycle regularly taken out!

indicators.note: letters are extracted at regular intervals, here every third one of the two words

explanation.surface: Therefore wheel your bike out for a ride on a routine basis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'regularly taken out' picks every third letter of push bicycle. The answer is the Latin for thus, printed after a quoted error.
explanation.definitionFit: A translation: the Latin word means thus.

clue.text: One's mad giving a clue like this

parts.note: one is a
mad means angry, which is cross

explanation.surface: Somebody must be crazy to offer a hint as odd as this.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition points at the clue itself, which runs horizontally in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: A self-reference: this clue is one of the horizontal entries.

clue.text: Thing that's essential to one's nearest and dearest

indicators.note: what is essential to something is at its core, so the letters lie inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Something that family and close friends cannot do without.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that's essential to' marks a run of letters inside nearest, and the same run sits inside dearest. The answer is the Latin for thing, used in law.
explanation.definitionFit: A translation: the Latin legal term for a matter or object.

clue.text: Kitchen accessories afterwards coming in cartons

indicators.note: coming in means entering, so the first piece goes inside the word for cartons

parts.note: cartons are packs, as of milk or juice
afterwards means later

explanation.surface: Gadgets for the cooking area are delivered in boxes at a future date.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming in' is the insertion signal; 'afterwards' reads as the surface's timing but is the piece that goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An example: they hold crockery upright to drain or store.

clue.text: Company banks new and old money in Tallinn

indicators.note: to bank is to deposit and hold, so the word for company holds the next piece

parts.note: a set is a company, a group of people who mix together

explanation.surface: A business pays in both the latest and the former currency in Estonia's capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banks' puts N inside SET. Tallinn is the capital of Estonia, whose kroon, used before the euro, was divided into a hundred of these.
explanation.definitionFit: A fact: it was the hundredth part of the Estonian kroon.
